en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 44, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then the lay follower Visākha approached the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā;
having approached, he paid homage to the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Visākha—
The lay follower said this to the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā:
“Venerable lady, it is said, ‘identity, identity.
What now, venerable lady, is this identity spoken of by the Blessed One?”
“Friend Visākha, these five aggregates of clinging have been called ‘identity’ by the Blessed One; that is to say:
the form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the volitional formations aggregate of clinging, and the consciousness aggregate of clinging.
These, friend Visākha, are the five aggregates of clinging that have been called ‘identity’ by the Blessed One.”
“Excellent, Venerable One,” said the lay follower Visākha, rejoicing and expressing his appreciation for what the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā had spoken. Then he asked her a further question:
“Venerable Lady, it is said, ‘the origin of identity, the origin of identity.
Now, Venerable Lady, what has been called by the Blessed One the origin of identity?”
“Friend Visākha, that craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—
that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence,
and craving for non-existence— this, friend Visākha, has been called the origin of identity by the Blessed One.”
“‘The cessation of identity, the cessation of identity,’ it is said, noble lady.
What now, noble lady, is called by the Blessed One the cessation of identity?
“That which, friend Visākha, is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving—its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment.”
“This, friend Visākha, is what the Blessed One has called the cessation of identity.
“Venerable lady, it is said: ‘The practice leading to the cessation of identity, the practice leading to the cessation of identity.
What, venerable lady, is this practice leading to the cessation of identity that has been spoken of by the Blessed One?”
“Friend Visākha, this very Noble Eightfold Path has been called by the Blessed One the way leading to the cessation of identity, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
“But, Venerable Lady, is that clinging itself the five aggregates of clinging, or is clinging something apart from the five aggregates of clinging?”
“Friend Visākha, clinging is neither identical to those five aggregates subject to clinging, nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging.
Whatever desire and lust there is for the five aggregates subject to clinging, that is the clinging therein.
“But how, noble lady, does identity view come to be?”
“Here, friend Visākha, an uninstructed worldling—unfamiliar with the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

unfamiliar with true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
He regards feeling … [and so on].”

One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as being in self, or self as being in perception. One regards volitional formations as self... one regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
“In this way, friend Visākha, there is identity view.
“But how, noble lady, is there no identity view?

“Here, friend Visākha, a well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the Noble Ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones; who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons—”
One does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
One does not [regard] feeling … nor perception … [in these ways].
One does not regard volitional formations as self...
nor consciousness as self, nor a self possessed of consciousness, nor consciousness within a self, nor a self within consciousness.
It is in this way, friend Visākha, that identity view does not exist.”
“But what, noble lady, is the Noble Eightfold Path?
“This, friend Visākha, is the Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
“But, noble lady, is the Noble Eightfold Path conditioned or unconditioned?
“The Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, is conditioned.
“Noble lady, are the three aggregates included within the Noble Eightfold Path, or is the Noble Eightfold Path included within the three aggregates?”
“Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not comprised within the Noble Eightfold Path; rather, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is comprised within the three aggregates.
Whatever is right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these phenomena are comprised within the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
Whatever is right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these phenomena are comprised within the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).”
“Right view and right intention—these phenomena are included within the aggregate of wisdom.
“But what, noble lady, is concentration? What phenomena are the signs of concentration? What phenomena are the requisites of concentration? What is the development of concentration?
“Friend Visākha, that one-pointedness of mind is concentration.”
The four foundations of mindfulness are the signs for concentration;
the four right endeavors are the requisites for concentration.
Whatever cultivation, development, and frequent practice there is of these very same states—this, in this context, is the development of concentration.”
“But how many, noble lady, are the formations?
“There are these three, friend Visākha:
the bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation.”
“But what, noble lady, is the bodily formation? What is the verbal formation? What is the mental formation?
“Breathing in and out, friend Visākha, is the bodily formation; applied thought and sustained thought are the verbal formation; perception and feeling are the mental formation.
“But why, noble lady, is breathing in and out the bodily formation? Why are applied thought and sustained thought the verbal formation? Why are perception and feeling the mental formation?”
“Friend Visākha, inhalation and exhalation are bodily phenomena bound up with the body; therefore, inhalation and exhalation are the bodily formation.
First, friend Visākha, one thinks and ponders, and afterwards one utters speech; therefore, thinking and pondering are the verbal formation.
Perception and feeling are mental phenomena bound up with the mind; therefore, perception and feeling are the mental formation.”
“But how, noble lady, does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling come about?
“Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu enters upon the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, it does not occur to him:

‘I shall enter upon the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I am entering upon the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I have entered upon the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.’”
“Then indeed his mind has been previously developed in such a way that it leads him to that state.
“But, Noble Lady, for a bhikkhu entering the cessation of perception and feeling, which phenomena cease first: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?
“For a bhikkhu, friend Visākha, entering the cessation of perception and feeling, first the verbal formation ceases, then the bodily formation, and then the mental formation.”
“But how, noble lady, does one emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling?
“Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, it does not occur to him:

‘I shall emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I am emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I have emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.’”
“Then indeed, his mind has previously been developed in such a way that it leads him to that state.

“But, noble lady, for a bhikkhu emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, which phenomena arise first: is it the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?

“For a bhikkhu, friend Visākha, emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, the mental formation arises first; after that, the bodily formation; and after that, the verbal formation.”
“But, noble lady, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, how many kinds of contact touch him?

“Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, three kinds of contact touch him: the void contact, the signless contact, and the desireless contact.
“But, noble lady, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, to what does his mind incline, to what does it lean, to what does it tend?”
“Friend Visākha, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, the mind inclines toward seclusion, tends toward seclusion, and leans toward seclusion.
“But lady, how many kinds of feeling are there?
“Friend Visākha, there are these three kinds of feeling:”
“Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
“But what, noble lady, is pleasant feeling? What is painful feeling? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
“Any bodily or mental feeling that is pleasant and agreeable, friend Visākha—”
This is pleasant feeling.
Whatever, friend Visākha, is felt as bodily or mental pain, as disagreeable—
this is painful feeling.
“Friend Visākha, whatever feeling—whether bodily or mental—is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, this is the feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

“But, Noble Lady, what is pleasant feeling pleasant for? What is pleasant feeling painful for? What is painful feeling pleasant for? What is painful feeling painful for? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling pleasant for? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling painful for?”
“Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is happiness in its persistence and suffering in its change;
painful feeling is suffering in its persistence and happiness in its change;
neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is happiness through knowledge and suffering through ignorance.”
“But, noble lady, what underlying tendency underlies pleasant feeling? What underlying tendency underlies painful feeling? What underlying tendency underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?

“Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust underlies pleasant feeling; the underlying tendency to aversion underlies painful feeling; the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

“Venerable lady, does the underlying tendency to lust underlie every pleasant feeling; does the underlying tendency to aversion underlie every painful feeling; and does the underlying tendency to ignorance underlie every neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
“Friend Visākha, it is not the case that the underlying tendency to lust underlies every pleasant feeling;
nor that the underlying tendency to aversion underlies every painful feeling; nor that the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies every neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

“But, noble lady, what is to be abandoned in regard to pleasant feeling? What is to be abandoned in regard to painful feeling? What is to be abandoned in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?

“Friend Visākha, in regard to pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to lust is to be abandoned; in regard to painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion is to be abandoned; in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to ignorance is to be abandoned.”

“Venerable lady, must the underlying tendency to lust be abandoned in regard to every pleasant feeling; the underlying tendency to aversion in regard to every painful feeling; and the underlying tendency to ignorance in regard to every neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
“Friend Visākha, it is not the case that the underlying tendency to lust must be abandoned in regard to every pleasant feeling;

nor that the underlying tendency to aversion must be abandoned in regard to every painful feeling; nor that the underlying tendency to ignorance must be abandoned in regard to every neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

"Here, friend Visākha, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
By means of that, he abandons lust; the underlying tendency to lust does not lie latent there.
Here, friend Visākha, a bhikkhu reflects thus:"
‘When indeed shall I attain and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now attain and dwell in?
Thus, for one who harbors a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, sorrow arises conditioned by that longing.
By means of that, he abandons aversion; no underlying tendency toward aversion lies latent therein.

"Here, friend Visākha, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
By this means he abandons ignorance; the underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie latent therein."
“But what, noble lady, is the counterpart to pleasant feeling?
“Painful feeling, friend Visākha, is the counterpart to pleasant feeling.
“But what, noble lady, is the counterpart to painful feeling?”
“Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is the counterpart to painful feeling.
“But, noble lady, what is the counterpart to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
“Friend Visākha, ignorance is the counterpart to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
“But what, noble lady, is the counterpart of ignorance?
“The counterpart of ignorance, friend Visākha, is true knowledge.
“But what, noble lady, is the counterpart of true knowledge?”
“Knowledge, friend Visākha, has liberation as its counterpart.
“But what, noble lady, is the counterpart of liberation?
“Liberation, friend Visākha, has Nibbāna as its counterpart.”
“But what, noble lady, is the counterpart of Nibbāna?
“You have gone too far with this question, friend Visākha; you were not able to grasp the limit of questions.
For the holy life, friend Visākha, is immersed in Nibbāna, culminates in Nibbāna, and finds its consummation in Nibbāna.”
“Friend Visākha, if you wish, go to the Blessed One and ask him about this matter; and whatever the Blessed One explains to you, you should bear that in mind.

Then the lay follower Visākha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for what the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā had said, rose from his seat, paid homage to the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā, and keeping her to his right, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the lay follower Visākha reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the lay follower Visākha:
“Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is wise; Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā possesses great wisdom.
If you had asked me this same matter, Visākha, I would have answered it in exactly the same way as the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has answered it.
Such indeed is its meaning, and so you should remember it.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The lay follower Visākha, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
